sources.ref_file_title: FLS90 - Multiple Non-Interactive Zero Knowledge Proofs Based on a Single Random String
sources.authors: Uriel Feige, Dror Lapidot, Adi Shamir
sources.note: cryptobib_key: FOCS:FeiLapSha90 (vendor/cryptobib/crypto.bib, pp. 308-317). Journal version: 'Multiple Non-Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs Under General Assumptions', SIAM J. Comput. 29(1):1-28, 1999, doi 10.1137/S0097539792230010 (not in cryptobib). Verifier: content confirmed via search snippets (NIZK for NP from certified trapdoor permutations for a polynomial-time prover, hidden-bits model, one string reused for polynomially many theorems); eprint/DBLP/ACM blocked by proxy.

Existing wiki page; its abstract: the enhancements 'arose in the study of Oblivious Transfer and NIZK ... we clarify why these enhancements are needed in such applications, and show that they actually suffice'.

sources.ref_file_title: BY96 - Certifying Permutations Noninteractive Zero-Knowledge Based on Any Trapdoor Permutation
sources.note: Added by verifier. cryptobib_key: JC:BelYun96 (pp. 149-166); conference version CRYPTO 1992 (C:BelYun92). Removes FLS90's certified-permutation hypothesis for families over bit strings by certifying the index with a NIZK proof. No key collision in existing-refs.txt.

cryptobib_key: TCC:CanLic18 (LNCS 11239, pp. 476-506). eprint 2017/631. Verifier: abstract confirmed via search snippets — identifies a gap in doubly enhanced TDPs regarding domain recognition and sampling, proposes 'certifiable injectivity', shows it suffices for the FLS paradigm even for trapdoor functions, and instantiates it from iO plus injective PRGs.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction: the reference string is parsed as permutation images, and prover and verifier call the family's index sampler, $\Eval$, $\Invert$, the certification procedure and the hard-core predicate only as oracles; the PRG for the multi-theorem step is built from the permutation by Goldreich-Levin, also as an oracle. One fixed reduction: soundness is statistical, and zero-knowledge is a hybrid over the hidden bits whose reduction runs any distinguisher as an oracle to predict the hard-core bit. Double enhancement and certification restrict the family $F_Q$; they do not give the construction non-oracle access to it. This is the RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.model_justification: The reference string carries the hidden bits; without it NIZK for $\classNP$ does not exist. Current value correct.
pages.statement: A family of doubly enhanced, certified [[trapdoor-permutation|trapdoor permutations]] (indices are recognizably permutations) yields a [[non-interactive-zero-knowledge|NIZK]] proof system for every language in $\classNP$ in the common reference string model: soundness is statistical, zero-knowledge is computational, and one reference string serves polynomially many theorems — [[FLS90 - Multiple Non-Interactive Zero Knowledge Proofs Based on a Single Random String|FLS90]]. The hidden-bits compilation uses the double enhancement, and double enhancement suffices for it — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]].
pages.sketch: FLS give an unconditional NIZK for Hamiltonicity in the hidden-bits model and compile it: the reference string is read as permutation images $y_1,\dots,y_m$, hidden bit $i$ is $b(\Invert(\td, y_i))$ for a hard-core predicate $b$, and the prover reveals a bit by publishing its preimage while unrevealed bits stay unpredictable to the verifier. One string serves polynomially many theorems by proving "$x \in L$ or the trailing block of the string is in the image of a $\PRG$"; the simulator plants a pseudorandom block and uses its seed as the witness.
pages.improvements_text:
- The hidden-bits compilation needs a doubly enhanced family, and double enhancement suffices — [[GR13 - Enhancements of Trapdoor Permutations|GR13]]
- For families over $\bits^n$ the certified-permutation hypothesis can be dropped: the prover certifies the index with a NIZK proof that it describes an (almost) permutation — [[BY96 - Certifying Permutations Noninteractive Zero-Knowledge Based on Any Trapdoor Permutation|BY96]]
- Doubly enhanced families still leave the FLS instantiation unsound for adversarially chosen indices whose domain is not recognizable; *certifiable injectivity* closes the gap and suffices for the FLS paradigm even for trapdoor functions — [[CL18 - Certifying Trapdoor Permutations, Revisited|CL18]]

pages.wrong_reason: The page asserts TDP ⇔ OT. The converse is false as far as is known: OT is not known to yield a trapdoor permutation, and the paper the migrated text quotes proves the opposite — GKM+00 (FOCS 2000) show that neither OT nor trapdoor predicates imply trapdoor permutations under black-box reductions, and that PKE and OT are black-box incomparable. The forward direction is also mis-stated: OT from trapdoor permutations needs an *enhanced* family, since the receiver must sample a domain element without learning its preimage. The migrated sentence 'TDPs (equivalently, the existence of PKE or OT)' fuses a disjunction into an equivalence, which the data model forbids. Delete this page: its only defensible content, enhanced TDP ⇒ OT, is already `content/Reductions/enhanced-trapdoor-permutations-to-ot-gkm-00.md`; downgrading to an implication would duplicate that edge.
flags: tdp-to-ot: HIGH — false equivalence; GKM+00 (existing wiki reference, abstract checked) rules out OT ⇒ TDP under black-box reductions. Recommend deletion; the surviving direction is `enhanced-trapdoor-permutations-to-ot-gkm-00`.

sources.venue: Journal of Computer and System Sciences 28(2), 1984
sources.note: Defines semantic security and builds bit-by-bit probabilistic encryption from any family of unapproximable trapdoor predicates; a trapdoor permutation with a hard-core predicate is such a family (predicate $b(f^{-1}(y))$, sampled by choosing $x$ with the wanted bit and outputting $f(x)$). Existing wiki page, cryptobib_key GolMic84.

sources.ref_file_title: GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions
sources.note: Supplies a hard-core predicate for every one-way, hence every trapdoor, permutation, so the hard-core bit is not an independent hypothesis of this edge.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction: $\KeyGen$ runs the family's index sampler, $\Enc$ calls $\Eval$ and the hard-core predicate, $\Dec$ calls $\Invert$, each only as an oracle. One fixed reduction: an $\indcpa$ adversary is run as an oracle to predict $b(x)$ from $f(x)$; for the Goldreich-Levin predicate the list-decoder turns that predictor into an inverter for $f$. RTV04 fully-black-box shape; current value retained.
pages.model_justification: No idealized model. Current value correct.
pages.statement: A family of [[trapdoor-permutation|trapdoor permutations]] $f$ with hard-core predicate $b$ gives an $\indcpa$-secure [[public-key-encryption|PKE]] scheme for one-bit messages: $\pk$ is the permutation index, $\sk$ its trapdoor, and $\Enc(\pk, m) = (f(x),\, b(x) \oplus m)$ for $x \getsr \calD$ — [[GM84 - Probabilistic encryption|GM84]], [[Yao82a - Theory and Applications of Trapdoor Functions|Yao82a]]. Every trapdoor permutation has a hard-core predicate, so no second hypothesis is needed — [[GL89 - A Hard-Core Predicate for All One-Way Functions|GL89]]; longer messages are encrypted bit by bit.
pages.sketch: Decryption recovers $x = \Invert(\sk, c_1)$ and outputs $c_2 \oplus b(x)$. An $\indcpa$ adversary distinguishing encryptions of $0$ from encryptions of $1$ predicts $b(x)$ from $f(x)$ with the same advantage, contradicting hard-coreness of $b$.

pages.wrong_reason: The migrated sentence is a definitional remark, not a reduction: it identifies the pseudorandomness property of a trapdoor PRG with that of $(\Gen,\Eval)$ read as a keyed PRG over $\calK \times \calT$. As an object-level equivalence the page is vacuous under the wiki's current definition: a trapdoor PRG is a PRG by dropping $\Invert$, and any PRG $G$ is a trapdoor PRG via $t = k = s$, $\Eval(t,k) = G(s)$, $\Invert(t,r) = [G(t) = r]$, because $\Eval$ is run once on the single pair drawn by $\Gen$. The hypothesis `trapdoor-pseudorandom-generator` is a variant anchor of `prg`, so the edge is also a self-loop. Delete the page and leave the sentence in the PRG page's Variations section. A trapdoor-PRG node needs a multi-sample definition first; after that, the two directions are separate edges.

sources.ref_file_title: BGW88 - Completeness theorems for non-cryptographic fault-tolerant distributed computation
sources.authors: Michael Ben-Or, Shafi Goldwasser, Avi Wigderson
sources.note: STOC 1988, pp. 1-10 (cryptobib STOC:BenGolWig88). Perfectly secure MPC for every function: t < n/2 passive, t < n/3 active, the latter via verifiable secret sharing of Shamir shares.

sources.ref_file_title: RB89 - Verifiable Secret Sharing and Multiparty Protocols with Honest Majority
sources.note: cryptobib_key: STOC:RabBen89 (pp. 73-85). Extends the VSS-to-MPC route to t < n/2 with statistical security given a broadcast channel. Verifier: existence and 'any multiparty protocol if a majority of the players are honest' confirmed via DBLP/search snippets; bibliographic data verified in cryptobib.

pages.class_justification: BGW88 predates the RTV04 vocabulary and states no reduction class; the protocol is information-theoretic, uses one specific VSS (bivariate polynomials) rather than an arbitrary VSS as an oracle, and has no adversary-as-oracle security reduction to place in the hierarchy.
pages.model_justification: No idealized model. The setting — pairwise private channels, unconditional security — is recorded in the statement rather than in `model`.
pages.statement: [[secret-sharing#verifiable-secret-sharing-vss|Verifiable secret sharing]] of degree-$t$ Shamir sharings, with a sub-protocol that multiplies two shared values and returns a degree-$t$ sharing of the product, gives perfectly secure [[secure-multi-party-computation|MPC]] for every function against a malicious adversary corrupting $t < n/3$ of the $n$ parties, over pairwise private channels — [[BGW88 - Completeness theorems for non-cryptographic fault-tolerant distributed computation|BGW88]].
pages.sketch: Each input is VSS-shared with a degree-$t$ polynomial; addition gates are local. For a multiplication gate each party VSS-shares the product of its two shares and the parties verify it, then take the Lagrange combination of these sub-sharings, which is a degree-$t$ sharing of the product. Reconstructing a degree-$t$ sharing with $t$ corrupted shares is Reed-Solomon decoding, which needs $n \ge 3t + 1$.
pages.improvements_text: - Given a broadcast channel and accepting statistical rather than perfect security, VSS with negligible error raises the threshold to $t < n/2$ — [[RB89 - Verifiable Secret Sharing and Multiparty Protocols with Honest Majority|RB89]]
notes_to_keep: The corruption threshold $t < n/3$ is a hypothesis of this result that the hyperedge does not carry; `content/Reductions/honest-majority-t-n-3-or-t-n-2-to-mpc-bgw88.md` records it as a separate edge.

This edge and `red-honest-majority-t-n-3-or-t-n-2-to-mpc-bgw88` are two halves of one theorem and should be merged into one conjunctive edge {verifiable-secret-sharing, t < n/3} ⇒ MPC.

sources.ref_file_title: LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices
sources.note: Pages 565-599; cryptobib_key DCC:LanSte15. eprint 2012/090. Abstract (confirmed via search snippet): a reduction from Mod-SIVP (SIVP restricted to module lattices) to Module-SIS, and a quantum reduction from Mod-SIVP to Module-LWE in both its search and decision versions.

pages.class_justification: A worst-case-to-average-case lattice reduction is not a construction of one primitive from another, so the RTV04 hierarchy does not apply; LS15 place it in no class. Matches the wiki's `sivp-to-lwe-reg05` and `ideal-svp-to-ring-lwe-lpr10`.
pages.model_justification: CHANGE REQUIRED: the page says `model: standard`. LS15's Module-LWE reduction is quantum (Regev's iterative quantum step); only the Module-SIS reduction in the same paper is classical. The wiki already uses `model: quantum` for `sivp-to-lwe-reg05` and `ideal-svp-to-ring-lwe-lpr10`.
pages.statement: Solving the shortest independent vectors problem on [[module-lattice-problems|rank-$d$ module lattices]] over the ring of integers of a degree-$n$ number field, in the worst case and to within polynomial approximation factors, reduces in quantum polynomial time to average-case [[learning-with-errors#module-lwe|Module LWE]] of rank $d$, in its search form and, for suitable moduli, its decision form — [[LS15 - Worst-case to average-case reductions for module lattices|LS15]]. Rank $d = 1$ is the [[learning-with-errors#ring-lwe|Ring LWE]] reduction and $n = 1$ recovers plain [[learning-with-errors|LWE]].
pages.sketch: Regev's iterative quantum step with $\ZZ^n$ replaced by a rank-$d$ module: the Module LWE oracle solves bounded-distance decoding on the dual module lattice, a quantum Fourier step turns that solver into a sampler of shorter discrete Gaussian vectors in the primal, and iterating drives the Gaussian width down to the target approximation factor.

sources.ref_file_title: GM24 - Edit Distance Robust Watermarks for Language Models
sources.note: Existing wiki page (cryptobib EPRINT:GolMoi24); NeurIPS 2024 title 'Edit Distance Robust Watermarks via Indexing Pseudorandom Codes' (proceedings entry found by search). Robustness to a constant fraction of adversarial insertions, substitutions and deletions, for alphabet size polynomial in the security parameter.

pages.class_justification: One fixed construction: generation calls the zero-bit PRC's $\Enc$ for a codeword and detection calls $\Dec$, both only as oracles. One fixed reduction: with uniform coins the generator's output is the model's own, so any distinguisher between watermarked and unwatermarked text is run as an oracle against PRC pseudorandomness; robustness is inherited from the PRC's channel robustness. RTV04 fully-black-box shape.
pages.model_justification: No idealized model; the language model is a parameter of the construction, not an oracle assumption. Current value correct.
pages.statement: A [[pseudorandom-error-correcting-code#zero-bit-prc|zero-bit PRC]] yields a [[language-model-watermarking|watermarking scheme]] for language models that is undetectable — any polynomial number of watermarked outputs is computationally indistinguishable from the model's own output — and whose detector survives cropping and a constant rate of random substitutions and deletions, provided the model's responses carry enough entropy — [[CG24 - Pseudorandom Error-Correcting Codes|CG24]].
pages.sketch: Generation samples the response using the bits of a fresh codeword $c \gets \Enc_k$ in place of uniform coins; with uniform coins the output is exactly the model's, so undetectability is PRC pseudorandomness. Detection recovers the sampling randomness from a candidate text and runs $\Dec_k$ on it; edits to the text act on that string as substitutions and deletions, which PRC robustness absorbs.

pages.class_justification: The map is the identity on algorithms and would be fully black-box, but it does not reach the conclusion as the wiki defines it: trapdoor-PRG soundness quantifies over every trapdoor, while PRC soundness fixes the string and averages over the key, so the identity map gives soundness only for all but a negligible fraction of trapdoors. No class is recorded until the two soundness definitions are aligned.

pages.statement: A zero-bit [[pseudorandom-error-correcting-code#zero-bit-prc|PRC]] $(\Gen, \Enc, \Dec)$ is a [[pseudorandom-generator#trapdoor-pseudorandom-generators|trapdoor pseudorandom generator]] with the PRC key as trapdoor $t$ and the encoder's coins as key $k$: $\Eval(t,k)$ runs $\Enc_t$ on coins $k$ and $\Invert(t,r) = [\Dec_t(r) \neq \bot]$. PRC pseudorandomness gives pseudorandomness, robustness at zero noise gives completeness, and PRC soundness gives soundness for all but a negligible fraction of trapdoors, since it fixes the string and averages over the key. PRC robustness makes completeness survive any $\varepsilon$-bounded channel — folklore.

zero-bit-prc-to-trapdoor-pseudorandom-generators: the migrated 'can be viewed as' is a viewpoint claim; the statement turns it into an explicit algorithm-by-algorithm and property-by-property correspondence, which is what makes the folklore label defensible.

u$, i.e. decoding almost never rejects. The inequality is inverted; CG24's soundness bounds false accepts, $\Pr_k[\Dec_k(\hat c) 
eq  ot] \le

zero-bit-prc-to-trapdoor-pseudorandom-generators: VERIFIER — class downgraded to `unstated`: the quantifier mismatch in soundness means the identity map does not meet the trapdoor-PRG definition as written, so recording a class would assert a reduction that does not exist exactly. Once the trapdoor-PRG soundness is averaged over $\Gen$ (or the PRC definition strengthened), the identity map is fully black-box.
